title: Labor Supply & Demand
description: How wages and hours emerge — substitution and income effects

concepts.title: Labor Demand
concepts.contentHtml:
Firms hire workers up to the point where the marginal value of an extra worker equals the wage they'd have to pay. Marginal Revenue Product of Labor (MRPL) — the extra revenue from one more worker — defines labor demand.

MRPL slopes downward in employment. With diminishing returns, each additional worker adds less to output. As more workers are hired, the marginal product falls, and firms keep hiring only as long as MRPL ≥ wage.

Higher wages reduce employment along the demand curve. Things that shift the curve: product demand (more demand → more workers needed), labor productivity (better technology raises MRPL), capital (more capital per worker raises MRPL).

concepts.title: Labor Supply
concepts.contentHtml:
Workers choose hours by trading off labor income and leisure time. Higher wages have two effects.

Substitution effect: leisure becomes more expensive in opportunity-cost terms, so workers substitute toward more work.

Income effect: higher wages mean each hour earns more, so workers can afford more leisure — pushing toward less work.

For most workers most of the time, substitution dominates and labor supply slopes upward. For very high earners, income effects sometimes dominate — labor supply curves can bend backward at the top.

Aggregate labor supply combines participation (extensive margin) and hours (intensive margin). Empirically, female labor supply is more elastic than male; secondary earners more than primary.

concepts.title: Equilibrium Wage
concepts.contentHtml:
The intersection of supply and demand gives the equilibrium wage w* and employment L*.

This is the textbook abstraction. Real labor markets have many frictions — search costs, location constraints, skill specificity — that prevent perfect equilibration.

Things that shift wages:

Demand shifts: productivity growth (positive), automation in routine tasks (negative for affected workers), trade competition (negative for import-competing sectors).

Supply shifts: immigration (positive for total employment, mixed for native wages), education and training, retirement waves.

The classical model is a starting point. Modern labor economics overlays it with search models, monopsony, human capital, and institutional frictions.

concepts.title: Compensating Differentials
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do underground miners earn more than office workers, even when the office workers are more skilled?

Adam Smith's answer: compensating differentials. Wages must compensate for non-wage features of jobs — danger, dirtiness, unpleasantness, social stigma, irregularity, location.

Workers don't simply maximize wages — they maximize total compensation, including the disutility of work. Higher pay can substitute for worse conditions; better conditions can offset lower pay.

Empirical estimates of compensating differentials for fatal injury risk anchor much of cost-benefit analysis in regulation. Estimates of 'value of statistical life' (VSL) typically run $9-13 million for US workers — derived from how much extra pay workers demand to take measurably riskier jobs.

Compensating differentials also explain wage gaps that aren't simple discrimination — flexibility, location, prestige, autonomy.

concepts.title: Frictions and Search
concepts.contentHtml:
Real labor markets aren't auctions. Workers and jobs match through a slow, costly search process.

Workers don't know where all openings are; firms don't know where suitable workers are. Both spend time searching, evaluating, and matching. The result: equilibrium unemployment can be positive even when the economy is otherwise at 'full employment.'

Search models (Diamond, Mortensen, Pissarides — Nobel 2010) formalize this. Wages, vacancies, and unemployment all emerge from a matching process with frictions.

This explains:

– Why unemployment doesn't go to zero even in booms.

– Why job-to-job transitions are common (better matches found over time).

– Why long-term unemployment is so harmful (skills atrophy, employers screen out long-jobless workers).

– Why labor market policy (unemployment insurance design, job training, hiring subsidies) has subtle effects on search behavior, not just static demand and supply.

title: Wage Determination
description: Minimum wages, monopsony, compensating differentials, efficiency wages

concepts.title: The Minimum Wage Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical model says binding minimum wages above market rates reduce employment — like any price floor.

Empirical evidence has been more mixed. The 1990s Card-Krueger study of NJ-PA minimum wage changes found no significant employment loss — even small positive effects.

Subsequent decades of research show: small minimum wage increases (10-20% above market) typically have small or zero employment effects. Large increases (50%+ above market) start showing real employment losses, especially among teens and the lowest-skilled.

The empirical pattern is more consistent with monopsony than perfect competition — modest minimum wages can transfer rents from employers to workers without disemploying them.

concepts.title: Monopsony in Labor Markets
concepts.contentHtml:
Monopsony is the labor-market equivalent of monopoly: a single (or dominant) employer in a local market. Modern usage extends to any setting where employers have wage-setting power.

A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply — to hire more workers, it has to pay more, including to existing workers. Marginal cost of labor exceeds the wage. The firm hires fewer workers and pays lower wages than competition would deliver.

Counterintuitive consequence: a minimum wage can raise employment if it's below the competitive level but above the monopsony level. This is the textbook resolution of the Card-Krueger findings.

Empirically, US labor markets show substantial monopsony power — Azar, Marinescu, Steinbaum (2020) find labor-market concentration is high in many local areas. Non-compete clauses, occupational licensing, and search frictions all amplify employer power. The 2020s have seen renewed antitrust interest in labor-market concentration.

concepts.title: Efficiency Wages
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do firms sometimes pay above market-clearing wages?

Efficiency wage theory: wages affect productivity. Pay above market and you get:

– Lower turnover (less recruiting cost).

– Higher effort (workers fear losing a 'good' job).

– Better applicants (adverse selection in reverse).

– Reduced shirking (Shapiro-Stiglitz model).

Henry Ford's $5 day in 1914 was famously above market — and Ford argued it raised productivity enough to be profitable. Modern Silicon Valley wages are partly efficiency wages.

The aggregate consequence: efficiency wages create involuntary unemployment. Firms pay above market because it's profitable; lower-wage workers can't bid jobs away. The 'natural rate' of unemployment incorporates this.

concepts.title: Unions and Collective Bargaining
concepts.contentHtml:
Labor unions act as monopoly sellers of labor — bargaining for higher wages, better conditions, employment protection.

Effects: unionized workers earn 10-20% higher wages on average than comparable non-union workers (the 'union wage premium'). Effects on employment depend on industry conditions; in monopsonistic settings, unions can offset employer power without job losses.

Distributional consequences: unions historically reduced wage inequality among the bottom 90% of workers. The decline of US union density (from ~30% in 1960 to ~10% now) is a significant contributor to rising wage inequality, per work by Card, Lemieux, and Riddell.

Trends: union density falling almost everywhere in the developed world. Sectoral shifts (manufacturing decline, services growth) drive much of the trend, but legal regimes (right-to-work laws, certification rules) matter too.

Rebound: 2020s saw renewed organizing in tech (Amazon, Starbucks), warehouses, and other previously non-union sectors — though early successes have faced fierce resistance.

concepts.title: Sticky Wages
concepts.contentHtml:
Wages adjust more slowly than prices in many markets. Wage stickiness is one of macroeconomics' most important features.

Sources: explicit contracts, implicit understandings, fairness norms (employees feel insulted by nominal wage cuts), morale effects, search costs.

Bewley (1999) interviewed firms during the 1990-91 recession and found pervasive resistance to nominal wage cuts. Firms preferred layoffs because cutting wages destroyed morale among remaining workers.

Macro consequences: nominal demand shocks affect output and employment, not just prices, because wages don't adjust fast enough. This is why monetary policy can have real effects in the short run.

Wage stickiness is asymmetric — wages rise more easily than they fall. Inflation can erode real wages painlessly; deflation forces a brutal adjustment. This is one reason central banks target positive inflation rather than zero — small inflation 'greases the wheels' of real wage adjustment.

title: Human Capital
description: Education, training, signaling vs productivity — Mincer equations

concepts.title: Human Capital Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Gary Becker's 1964 framework: education and training are investments. Workers acquire skills now to earn higher wages later.

The decision: invest if and only if the present value of future wage increases exceeds the cost (tuition + foregone earnings + effort).

This frames education as economic choice subject to the same NPV logic as any other investment. It explains:

– Why young people get more education than old (more years to recoup).

– Why education is greater in low-mortality societies.

– Why subsidies raise enrollment.

– Why credit constraints matter (binding constraints prevent positive-NPV investments).

Human capital theory dominated labor economics for decades. It's been complicated by signaling theory but never replaced.

concepts.title: The Mincer Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacob Mincer's 1974 specification: log wage = α + β·schooling + γ·experience + δ·experience² + ε.

The coefficient β is the return to a year of schooling. Across countries and decades, OLS estimates of β are typically 0.06-0.10 — each year of schooling associated with 6-10% higher earnings.

Mincer earnings functions are the workhorse of labor economics empirics. They form the basis of returns-to-education estimates, education subsidies cost-benefit analysis, and human-capital growth accounting.

OLS estimates have known biases. Smarter people get more schooling and earn more for both reasons; OLS conflates the two. IV estimates using compulsory schooling laws or other exogenous schooling shifters often find similar or somewhat larger effects, supporting the view that schooling has real causal returns.

concepts.title: Signaling vs Skill-Building
concepts.contentHtml:
Spence's 1973 challenge: maybe education's wage premium reflects sorting more than skill-building. High-ability workers find education less costly and self-select into more of it. Employers infer ability from education even if education itself didn't add much.

The pure signaling view says school doesn't make you more productive; it just identifies who was already productive. Bryan Caplan's 'Case Against Education' makes this argument strongly.

The mainstream view: both effects matter, but they're hard to separate. Some skills clearly are taught (medicine, engineering, accounting). Others (general knowledge, abstract reasoning) might be either. Returns to education in liberal arts and humanities are puzzling for pure human-capital views.

Empirically: schooling that delivers measurable skills (vocational, STEM, professional) shows strong returns. General education's returns may be partly signaling, but the evidence for substantial human-capital effects is also strong. Pure signaling can't explain why education effects show up on cognitive tests, not just wages.

concepts.title: Specific vs General Human Capital
concepts.contentHtml:
Becker distinguished two types of training.

General human capital: useful at any employer (literacy, programming, leadership). Workers should pay for it themselves; firms won't, since workers can leave and take the training elsewhere.

Firm-specific human capital: only useful at one firm (knowledge of company processes, internal relationships). Firms should pay for it. Workers and firms share the returns to keep both committed to the relationship.

The mix shapes wages and turnover. High-specificity jobs feature long tenures, internal labor markets, and shared investment. Low-specificity jobs feature high turnover, external labor markets, and worker-financed training.

Modern shifts: as job-specific knowledge becomes harder to keep proprietary (with documentation, software, standardization), specific human capital may be declining as a share. This contributes to shorter average tenures.

concepts.title: Returns to Education and Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
The college wage premium — average college-graduate earnings divided by high-school-graduate earnings — has roughly doubled in the US since 1980, from ~50% to ~80%.

Why? Skill-biased technical change. Computers and information technology complement skilled labor and substitute for routine labor. The result: rising returns to skills that computers can't replace, declining returns to those they can.

This explains the U-shaped distribution of US labor-market changes since 1980 (Autor): demand for high-skill professional and managerial jobs has risen, demand for low-skill service jobs has held up, but middle-skill routine jobs (clerical, manufacturing) have hollowed out.

The implication: returns to education aren't just about the average effect — they're about what skills the education actually delivers. STEM and professional degrees show very high returns; general arts degrees show smaller and flatter returns.

The college wage premium has actually flattened since 2010-15. Combined with rising tuition, the marginal return to college has compressed for many. Whether this is a temporary plateau or a structural shift remains debated.

title: Unemployment Theory
description: Frictional, structural, cyclical — search models, matching, hysteresis

concepts.title: Why Unemployment Exists
concepts.contentHtml:
In the textbook model with flexible wages, there's no involuntary unemployment — anyone willing to work at the market wage finds a job.

Real economies have unemployment everywhere. Why?

Wage rigidities: wages don't fall fast enough to clear the market.

Search frictions: finding the right job-worker match takes time.

Efficiency wages: firms deliberately pay above market to motivate effort and reduce turnover.

Insider-outsider effects: employed workers have bargaining power; the unemployed don't.

Each mechanism explains some of observed unemployment. Together they account for why developed economies typically run unemployment between 3% (very tight) and 12% (deep recession), never zero.

concepts.title: Search and Matching Models
concepts.contentHtml:
The Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides framework (Nobel 2010) is the dominant model of unemployment dynamics.

Workers search for jobs; firms search for workers. They meet through a matching function M(u, v) where u is unemployment and v is vacancies. The function exhibits constant returns to scale and depends on labor market institutions, geography, and information.

The Beveridge curve plots vacancies against unemployment. In normal times it traces a downward-sloping curve — high vacancies imply low unemployment.

Outward shifts of the curve indicate matching has gotten worse — for a given vacancy level, unemployment is higher. The post-2009 US Beveridge curve shifted out, signaling deeper structural problems. The 2022 curve shifted dramatically, with very high vacancies but moderate unemployment — a tight labor market with mismatch.

concepts.title: The Natural Rate
concepts.contentHtml:
The natural rate of unemployment (or NAIRU) is the level the economy gravitates toward when expectations have caught up. A combination of frictional, structural, and efficiency-wage components.

It's not a fixed number. NAIRU shifts with:

– Demographics (younger workers have higher unemployment).

– Industrial structure (rapid sectoral change raises structural unemployment).

– Labor market institutions (UI generosity, EPL, minimum wages).

– Skill mismatches.

– Labor force participation patterns.

US NAIRU was estimated at ~6% in the 1980s, ~5% in the 1990s-2000s, possibly ~4% in 2015-19. Estimates are uncertain — a CBO study showed estimated NAIRU 1-percentage-point-wide confidence intervals.

The natural rate is what monetary policy can't push below sustainably without accelerating inflation. Trying to do so triggered the 1970s stagflation.

concepts.title: Hysteresis
concepts.contentHtml:
Hysteresis in labor markets: temporary unemployment shocks become permanent. The cyclical and the structural blur together.

Mechanisms: long-term unemployed lose skills and motivation. Employers screen out the long-jobless. Networks weaken. Workers leave the labor force entirely.

Europe in the 1980s-90s was the textbook case: unemployment rose during the early-1980s recession and stayed high for two decades. Some of what looked like 'natural rate' was actually permanent damage from earlier cyclical shocks.

Implications: aggressive demand stimulus during recessions can prevent hysteresis from setting in — what looks like 'overheating' may simply be preventing permanent labor-market damage.

The 2010s slow US recovery, vs the 2021-22 fast recovery, may turn out to be a natural experiment in hysteresis. Early evidence suggests the fast recovery did avoid the labor-force-detachment problems of the prior cycle.

concepts.title: Unemployment Insurance and Active Labor Market Policy
concepts.contentHtml:
Government interventions in labor markets target three goals: income support, search incentives, and efficient matching.

Unemployment Insurance (UI): short-term income replacement. Trade-off: more generous → less search effort, longer durations. Empirically, modest UI (50-60% replacement, 6-12 months) provides large welfare gains for small disincentive costs.

Active Labor Market Policies (ALMP): training, job-search assistance, hiring subsidies, public employment services. Effectiveness varies. Job-search assistance generally helps; large training programs often disappoint relative to costs.

Employment Protection Legislation (EPL): rules around firing, severance, notice periods. Strong protection raises tenure for incumbents but reduces hiring; effect on aggregate employment is ambiguous.

Wage subsidies (EITC): top up earnings for low-wage workers. Highly effective at boosting employment and reducing poverty. Earned Income Tax Credit is the largest US anti-poverty program for working-age adults.

The Nordic 'flexicurity' model — flexible firing rules, generous UI, strong ALMP — is often cited as a successful synthesis. Replicating it elsewhere has been difficult, but its components have been widely adopted.

title: Discrimination & Inequality
description: Becker's model, statistical discrimination, gender and racial gaps, immigration effects

concepts.title: Becker's Taste-Based Discrimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Gary Becker's 1957 model: some employers have a 'taste' for discrimination — they pay extra (in foregone profits) to avoid hiring certain groups.

Key prediction: in competitive markets, taste-based discrimination is unstable. Non-discriminating employers face lower labor costs, gain market share, drive out the discriminators. Competitive pressure should erode discrimination over time.

The empirical record is mixed. Discrimination has reduced over decades — black-white wage gaps narrowed dramatically post-1965. But persistent gaps remain that aren't easily explained by taste-based theory in competitive markets.

This motivated alternative theories that didn't predict discrimination would self-extinguish.

concepts.title: Statistical Discrimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Phelps and Arrow's 1970s model: employers can't perfectly observe individual productivity. They use group averages as predictors.

If average productivity differs (or appears to differ) across groups, it can be 'rational' for employers to discount applicants from the lower-average group — even when the individual applicant is high-productivity.

This is statistical discrimination. It can persist in competitive markets because no individual employer has reason to deviate from the statistical inference.

Self-fulfilling prophecies: if discriminated-against groups invest less in education or career commitment because they expect lower returns, the statistical pattern reinforces itself.

The harder problem with statistical discrimination: it's not always factually wrong about averages. The remedy isn't proving employers wrong about base rates — it's the law's blanket prohibition on using race, sex, etc. in employment decisions even when statistically informative.

concepts.title: Gender Wage Gaps
concepts.contentHtml:
The raw gender wage gap (women earn ~80-85¢ per dollar earned by men in many developed countries) shrinks substantially when controls are added.

Major contributors:

– Occupation choice: women are overrepresented in lower-paid sectors (caregiving, education, retail). Why is itself contested.

– Hours and continuity: women average fewer hours and more career interruptions, especially around childbirth.

– The 'motherhood penalty': Goldin's research shows the gap accelerates after first birth and never fully closes.

– Compensating differentials: women on average choose more flexible, lower-pay jobs — possibly because of social norms, possibly preferences.

Claudia Goldin's Nobel-winning work (2023) emphasizes the role of 'greedy jobs' — high-pay positions requiring inflexible long hours — as the persistent driver. Where flexibility is high (pharmacy, some tech jobs), gender gaps are small. Where it's low (law, finance, surgery), gaps are large.

The remaining within-occupation, within-experience gap (~5-10%) is harder to explain by anything but discrimination, though even that remains debated.

concepts.title: Racial Wage Gaps
concepts.contentHtml:
US racial wage gaps narrowed substantially 1940-1980, especially during 1960s civil rights era. Since 1980, the convergence has stalled or reversed.

Audit studies (Bertrand-Mullainathan 2004) sent identical résumés with stereotypically white vs black names. White-named applications received 50% more callbacks. The methodology is now standard for documenting hiring discrimination.

Components of the gap:

– Pre-market factors: different educational quality, family wealth, neighborhood effects, intergenerational transmission of disadvantage.

– Hiring discrimination: documented, persistent, robust to many controls.

– Wage discrimination: smaller within firms but real.

– Promotion gaps: 'glass ceilings' visible in management and executive ranks.

The Chetty et al. work using IRS data documents that black men in particular face very low intergenerational mobility — even children of high-income black families end up with sharply lower lifetime earnings than white peers. This suggests labor-market discrimination is layered on top of broader social and family dynamics.

concepts.title: Immigration's Wage Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
Does immigration reduce native wages?

Theoretical answer: maybe a little, in the short run, for workers who compete directly with immigrants.

Empirical answer is more nuanced. Card's 1990 Mariel boatlift study (large unexpected influx of Cubans to Miami) found minimal wage effects. Borjas's reanalysis found larger negative effects on low-skill native workers. The debate continues.

Modern consensus: aggregate effects of immigration on native wages are small — maybe -1 to -2% in the short run, dissipating over time. Distributional effects matter more than aggregate ones. Low-skill immigrants compete with low-skill natives, slightly lowering their wages. High-skill immigrants complement natives more often than they substitute.

Long-run effects are clearly positive: immigrants add to GDP, pay taxes, fill labor shortages, often start businesses. The fiscal calculation depends on skill mix and tax-and-benefit structures. High-skill immigration is fiscally positive almost everywhere; low-skill effects depend on country-specific welfare design.

Politics aside, the economic case for moderate immigration is strong. The political backlash against immigration in many democracies hasn't tracked the underlying economics.
